text: Almost every SOC starts out purely reactive, only investigating and responding to alerts as correlation rules raise them. That's a reasonable place to begin, but it has a real limitation this lesson walks through, along with the concrete practices that actually move a SOC from reactive toward genuinely proactive over time.

A purely reactive SOC's limitation shows up clearly with a slow, deliberate data exfiltration that stays just under every threshold a correlation rule checks for. Nothing ever fires, so nothing is ever reviewed — the exfiltration can continue indefinitely, not because any analyst missed it, but because no alert ever existed in the first place for anyone to see. The SOC can be fully staffed and still miss it, because staffing only helps once something actually surfaces.

A proactive SOC adds three things on top of alert response: threat hunting, deliberately searching for compromise that existing rules wouldn't catch; continuous improvement, turning what hunts and real incidents reveal into new, tuned correlation rules; and metrics-driven management, tracking mean time to detect and mean time to respond so the SOC knows objectively whether it's actually getting faster.

Maturity isn't a single flip — no SOC gets promoted from reactive to proactive overnight. Practices get layered on top of the reactive baseline as staffing and experience grow: first handle the queue reliably, then tune rules based on what hunts and incidents reveal, then add dedicated hunting time, then track metrics to drive real decisions with leadership. Most real SOCs sit somewhere in between for a long time, with only pieces of proactive practice layered onto an otherwise reactive core.

That closes Chapter 1 — the mission, the tiers that staff it, the shifts that cover it, and the maturity that improves it over time. Chapter 2 opens with the tool nearly every one of those practices actually runs on day to day: what a SIEM actually does, and how it makes everything in this chapter possible in practice.
